\title{LLM-to-Map: Conversational Co-Simulation of Power and Transportation Networks via LLM-Driven Map Control}

\begin{abstract}
We present \textbf{LLM-to-Map}, a conversational interface for controlling and exploring a co-simulation of urban infrastructures. The system integrates SUMO for microscopic traffic modeling and PyPSA for electrical grid simulation, synchronized through an event-driven coordination engine that captures cascading effects between domains. A novel temporal dynamics system enables continuous time progression (e.g., 08:00 $\rightarrow$ 08:01 $\rightarrow$ 08:02) with intelligent vehicle quota management that automatically maintains realistic traffic density as vehicles reach destinations throughout nine time-based patterns (rush hour, midday, night). An LLM agent powered by GPT-4 provides natural language interaction, translating user queries into simulator actions and visualization commands. LLM-to-Map supports fault-tolerant geospatial search, infrastructure control (e.g., triggering substation failures, activating vehicle-to-grid responses), and interactive map navigation. The Unity/Mapbox visualization layer renders disruptions and recovery processes in real-time. We showcase three scenarios: (1) EV charging stress on substations, (2) grid outage cascading into traffic disruptions, and (3) V2G-enabled resilience. By combining adaptive co-simulation with conversational control, LLM-to-Map lowers the barrier to studying cross-network resilience. Check our demo at \href{https://github.com/XGraph-Team/Map-LLM}{\faGithub\ Github.com/XGraph-Team/Map-LLM}.
\end{abstract}

\maketitle

\section{Introduction}
Urban infrastructures rarely operate in isolation. Transportation networks depend on electricity for traffic signals and EV charging, while power grids rely on mobility patterns. Disruptions cascade between domains: substation failures disable intersections, and traffic congestion delays grid repair. Domain simulators like SUMO~\cite{lopez2018sumo} and PyPSA~\cite{brown2018pypsa} excel within domains, and co-simulation frameworks such as GEMINI~\cite{panossian2023architecture} and V2Sim~\cite{qian2024v2sim} couple networks. However, these require technical expertise and restrict interaction to fixed parameters.

LLMs enable conversational interfaces for complex systems, explored in smart city decision support~\cite{kalyuzhnaya2025llm} and urban planning~\cite{han2025large}, with surveys highlighting potential in multi-agent control~\cite{guo2024large}.

We introduce \textbf{LLM-to-Map}, combining co-simulation of power and traffic networks with an LLM-driven conversational interface and continuous temporal dynamics. Users issue commands such as "turn off Penn Station substation" or "set time to 8" and observe real-time impacts. Progressive time initiates temporal flow where simulation time advances continuously (08:00 $\rightarrow$ 08:01...), while intelligent vehicle quota management maintains traffic patterns by spawning replacements as vehicles complete trips. This transforms static scenarios into living urban simulation supporting long-term resilience studies. The demo showcases grid-traffic cascades, EV charging stress, and V2G stabilization.

\section{System Overview}
The \textbf{LLM-to-Map} framework consists of three core layers: (1) domain simulators, (2) coordination engine with temporal dynamics, and (3) interaction and visualization layer (Figure~\ref{fig:structure}).

\begin{figure}[t]
    \centering
    \includegraphics[width=0.95\linewidth]{co-sim.pdf}
    \caption{System architecture: SUMO and PyPSA synchronized by event-driven coordination with progressive time and vehicle quota manager. LLM agent (GPT-4) interprets natural language and controls Unity/Mapbox visualization.}
    \label{fig:structure}
\end{figure}

\noindent\textbf{Domain Simulators.}
We integrate SUMO for microscopic transport modeling~\cite{lopez2018sumo} and PyPSA for electrical network analysis~\cite{brown2018pypsa}. SUMO models central Manhattan (34th–59th Street) with hundreds of edges, intersections, and actuated signals. EVs are represented with battery state-of-charge tracking. PyPSA represents eight major substations (600–1000 MVA) connected to transmission nodes, transformers, and loads, accounting for baseline demand and dynamic EV charging with power flow solved every five seconds.

\noindent\textbf{Temporal Dynamics and Resource Management.}
LLM-to-Map implements a progressive time system where setting a time initiates continuous temporal flow (08:00 $\rightarrow$ 08:01 $\rightarrow$ 08:02...). The system maintains nine time-based traffic patterns, each defining vehicle quotas (10–100) and EV penetration rates (50–75\%). An intelligent quota manager monitors vehicle counts every 5 seconds, spawning replacements when vehicles reach destinations, ensuring realistic traffic density. For example, during morning rush (7–9 AM), the system maintains 85–100 vehicles; if count drops to 80, it spawns 5 more with appropriate EV ratios. This transforms the platform into a living, self-sustaining urban simulation for long-term resilience studies.

\noindent\textbf{Event-Driven Coordination.}
A Python engine synchronizes SUMO and PyPSA through a shared clock. Events propagate across domains: substation failures disable traffic lights, EV charging aggregates into substation loads, and overloads trigger alerts. This design preserves causality and supports cascading effects.

\noindent\textbf{LLM-to-Map Interaction Layer.}
A GPT-4~\cite{achiam2023gpt} + LangChain agent processes natural language instructions and maps them to infrastructure or visualization commands. Examples include "turn off Penn Station substation" (grid failure cascades), "show me Times Square" (camera navigation), and "activate vehicle-to-grid rescue" (EVs discharge energy). The system employs fuzzy string matching (Levenshtein distance $\leq$2) for typo-tolerant location retrieval.

\noindent\textbf{Visualization and Playback.}
The Unity/Mapbox interface renders Manhattan in 3D, overlaying grid nodes, traffic signals, and EV stations. Disruptions and recovery actions are animated with flashing outages, EV discharges, and cinematic camera transitions. The interface supports both free exploration and scripted scenario playback for expert analysis and public demonstrations.

\section{Demonstration Scenarios}
We illustrate the system through three scenarios highlighting power-transportation interdependence. Scenarios are launched via natural language commands with effects visualized in real-time (Figure~\ref{fig:interface}).

\par\noindent
\begin{minipage}{\columnwidth}
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.9\columnwidth]{Screenshot.png}
\captionof{figure}{LLM-to-Map interface showing Manhattan testbed with substations, traffic signals, and conversational chatbot control panel.}
\label{fig:interface}
\end{minipage}

\noindent\textbf{Scenario 1: EV Charging Stress.}
This scenario explores how high EV penetration stresses distribution substations. Vehicles spawn with 25–30\% battery, immediately seeking charging. Users trigger "blackout scenario," failing all substations except one. The camera zooms out to show sequential failures across the network, then focuses on the sole operational station. As simulation time progresses (e.g., 08:00 $\rightarrow$ 08:30), the progressive time system automatically maintains rush-hour vehicle quotas (85–100), continuously spawning replacements as vehicles complete trips. This sustained pressure persists throughout the rush period, with all EVs converging on one location. The station rapidly reaches capacity, creating visible queuing patterns with vehicles circling while the camera captures their desperate search for charging. Some become stranded as batteries deplete. This demonstrates the feedback loop from mobility behavior into grid stress, emphasizing infrastructure redundancy importance during emergencies (Figure~\ref{fig:scenario1}).

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{scenario2.png}
\caption{Scenario 1: Blackout stress test. (1) Normal grid operation: all 8 substations functional, distributed EV charging load; (2) Critical infrastructure failure: single substation operational (1/8); (3) System response: all EVs rerouting to single station, capacity reached (20/20 occupied), queue formation visible; (4) Critical impact: multiple vehicles stranded (battery depleted), unable to access overloaded charging station.}
\label{fig:scenario1}
\end{figure}

\noindent\textbf{Scenario 2: Grid-Induced Charging Disruptions.}
A user types "turn off Penn Station substation," immediately disabling all charging stations in that service area. Vehicles attempting to charge reroute to operational stations, creating localized queues and circling behavior. Vehicles unable to secure charging risk battery depletion and stranding. PyPSA reflects load loss and demand redistribution. Users can restore substations via "restore Penn Station" or "restore all" commands, instantly re-enabling charging infrastructure. This scenario demonstrates how single grid outages cascade into widespread mobility disruptions (Figure~\ref{fig:scenario2}).

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.75\columnwidth]{scenario1.png}
\caption{Scenario 2: Grid-induced charging disruption. (1) Pre-command state: Penn Station substation online, normal grid operations; (2) Post-command impact: Penn Station substation offline, area affected, power disrupted.}
\label{fig:scenario2}
\end{figure}

\noindent\textbf{Scenario 3: Vehicle-to-Grid Rescue.}
V2G is activated as a resilience measure. Users type "run V2G scenario," triggering Times Square substation failure with people trapped in an elevator. The system identifies nearby EVs with battery $\geq$70\%, sending compensation-incentivized discharge requests. Vehicles spawn with high battery levels to ensure participation. The camera zooms to the failed substation, showing EVs responding, connecting to discharge points, and collectively injecting power. Aggregated injection raises voltages, restores substation operation, frees trapped occupants, and brings signals online. Unity/Mapbox visualizations show EVs rerouting to V2G-enabled stations, with restored signals flashing green. The chatbot provides comprehensive session summaries including total power restored, participating vehicles, and compensation earned. This scenario demonstrates how EVs transform from grid stressors to stabilizers during emergencies (Figure~\ref{fig:scenario3}).

\begin{figure}[H]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.95\columnwidth]{scenario3.png}
\caption{Scenario 3: V2G emergency response. (1) Normal operation: Times Square substation online; (2) Substation failed: 18 people trapped in elevators; (3) V2G active: EVs (>70\% charge) discharging power for payment; (4) V2G success: power restored, elevators and traffic signals online.}
\label{fig:scenario3}
\end{figure}

\noindent\textbf{Interactive Exploration.}
While scenarios can be played in scripted form, the demo supports exploration. Attendees may combine scenarios or issue free-form queries such as "zoom to Grand Central and show traffic impact." The LLM agent interprets conversational inputs, executes simulator actions, and returns synchronized visualizations. This transforms the demo into a live laboratory for studying cascading failures and resilience strategies.

\section{Discussion and Outlook}
The \textbf{LLM-to-Map} system demonstrates how conversational interfaces bridge the gap between technical co-simulation tools and accessible urban analysis. By integrating SUMO, PyPSA, and Unity/Mapbox under a common event-driven engine with progressive temporal dynamics, the system captures bidirectional effects between networks while maintaining realistic traffic patterns through intelligent resource management. The LLM agent lowers interaction barriers, enabling users to trigger outages, observe cascading failures, and activate V2G responses without domain expertise.

The architecture is generalizable: any city with OpenStreetMap and utility data can be incorporated, and the modular design allows additional infrastructures (communication, water, supply chains) to be added as plugins. From a research perspective, the system contributes to both web search (fuzzy geospatial retrieval, conversational state tracking) and urban computing (interactive resilience analysis). For practitioners, it offers hands-on decision support making cascading risks and mitigation strategies visible in real time. We envision LLM-to-Map evolving into a collaborative platform where researchers, operators, and citizens explore smart city resilience together.
